title: Wildcard support in Logstash pipelines search API.

timeline.body:
## What is happening?
`_logstash/pipeline?id={}` API does not support searching pipelines by `wildcard IDs`.

**Why it is important?**
Currently, every Logstash instance fetches all pipelines (from `.logstash` index) every 5s (configurable) and filters locally based on Logstash instance pipeline settings. Pipeline config may include wildcard IDs. After this change, every Logstash instance should consider ROI pipelines config. That's said, LS instance sends its pipeline IDs to Elasticsearch and gets the pipeline configs only belong to itself. This dramatically decreases network load as well as gives an opportunity to control pipelines in dynamic way with wildcards.

### Issue
Closes #84772

## Does Kibana get affected by this change?
- **NO**: we are not changing API interface, extending its behavior.

## Documentation
- No change required in [Elasticsearch (Kibana CPM) ](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/kibana/8.2/logstash-configuration-management-api.html)side since no feature affected in Kibana.
- Logstash team documents when client side behavior/code changes (after merging this PR).

## Acceptance Criteria
API should support wildcard IDs and return pipeline configs based on requested IDs (explicit and wildcard).

## Solution
We had two solution approaches:
- fetching all docs from `.logstash` index and filter based on requested ID.
- support wildcard ES query
Why we choose #option 1? - Based on team's decision ([RFC](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1NtTB0L9oBno4yEjpr8PkliFSMV8JXa5silyBizFZxJw)), customers are less affected.

### Tests
#### Prerequisites
- Make sure you cloned the Elasticsearch repo
- Make sure you installed Kibana on your local machine
- Make sure you cloned the Logstash repo (required LS to ES communication)
- Make sure python is installed on your local machine
- Run Elasticsearch with `./gradlew :run`
- Go to Postman and send a request to generate Kibana token, add user name & password to Basic auth header.
`POST: localhost:9200/_security/service/elastic/kibana/credential/token/kibanaToken`
- Set received Kibana token to kibana.yml under the Kibana config folder
- Run the Kibana and go to the Stack Management -> Users page. Note that default authentication will be uid: elastic, pwd: password when accessing the Kibana.
- Create a user named logstash with logstash-admin & logstash-system roles. They will be required to directly access the .logstash index.
- Run the [python script](https://gist.github.com/mashhurs/79441a7380ae18c32931dc544ec549ab) to generate bunch of pipelines

#### Test
- Now you can go to Postman and do wildcard pipelines search, eg.:
`GET http://localhost:9200/_logstash/pipeline?id=ry*,rob*,ki*chy*`
I will change this to static.
I need to remove special chars since Kibana also does not allow special chars for pipeline name.

I have a concern about the user experience of wildcard pattern across Logstash and Elasticsearch. 

Currently Logstash accept alphabet, number, `_`, `-` as pipeline id and only accept `*` as wildcard to match any character in pipeline id. For example pattern `*mashhur*` matches `mashhur123`, `123mashhur456`
The proposed API translate `*` -> `.*` to be a regex pattern, which means it accepts other special characters like `+`, `.`, `?`. (1) Although this pattern looks very similar to regex, it is not exactly the same because of `*` -> `.*` translation. This is confusing to the user. 

Another confusion is the inconsistent behavior of Logastash and Elasticsearch. Users want to get pipelines from a wildcard pattern. (2) They face different syntax to get the same content. For example Elasticsearch API accept `mash+ur*` to match `mashhur` while Logstash throw exception because of special character `+`.

I would suggest to unify the user experience by either accept regex in API and Logstash config (a breaking change) or escape the special character in API so it only consider `*` in matching.

Thanks @kaisecheng for good points.
I was also aware of your 2nd point (pipeline search worked when I sent regex patter through URL query string). Plz take a look at my latest (`Wildcard regex pattern improvement`) commit so that it covers both your concerns.

My opinion for your additional following point would be "we assume users are installed standard (not customized) Logstash and Elasticsearch and the API gets the validated pipelines by [Logstash bootstrap check](https://github.com/elastic/logstash/blob/611953bbe96b4178bfbec5029e127af880ee0fa7/x-pack/lib/config_management/bootstrap_check.rb#L19) and Kibana UI validation." Let me plz know if you think we should check pattern anywhere in all pipelines related ES APIs. I think it is not necessary unless there should be a strict reason to really block this case.
```
Currently Logstash accept alphabet, number, _, - as pipeline id and only accept * as wildcard to match any character in pipeline id.
```

I agree with you that we don't need to give pattern checking to all APIs in this enhancement. The goal is to bring wildcard to search system index. Logstash do not have upsert feature to central management. So, aligning the search part is good enough for now. It is nice to have for future to align Kibana and Elasticsearch API.

Thanks @kaisecheng for the details,
If you are worrying about performance, as my understanding it will not matter since JIT optimizer takes care.
From clean code perspective, it really varies from person to person. My approach is based on lambda where I use `filter` and `map` in plain loop as well. Where I am filtering by continuing and mapping at the end. If we have strict code formatting I am happy to change.

timeline.body:
Good improvement for the wildcard handling. The search experience aligns with Logstash now. One suggestion is to have unit test for wildcard matching part.

For example
pipeline ids: super_generator, another_generator, hello
pattern: *generator
matching result: super_generator, another_generator

This method is going to compile the pattern every time it is executed, which seems like a pretty tight loop. I think we should compile all the patterns that will be used for matching in an earlier phase.
Since we assign a new variable later to hold this value (`finalNumHitsToFetch`) can we instead make a new variable here to hold this mutation instead of overwriting the parameter passed in?

I think we can check for this failure scenario before iterating over the records from this scroll response. I think it'd be better to error out earlier in that case and save the work of checking against patterns.

Variable name is a little confusing here, can we make this something like "numberOfHitsSeenSoFar"? Then the method parameter could be something like "numberOfHitsSeenPreviously"?

The name "maxNumHitsToFetch" makes me think this is a hard limit on the results, but in reality it's just a counter and the hard limit is the scroll total hits.

reply.body:
Couldn't figure out why my test case `testGetPipelinesByExplicitAndWildcardIds` is causing thread leak. Do you have any idea?

```
// log
com.carrotsearch.randomizedtesting.ThreadLeakError: 1 thread leaked from SUITE scope at org.elasticsearch.xpack.logstash.action.TransportGetPipelineActionTests: 
   1) Thread[id=24, name=elasticsearch[testGetPipelinesByExplicitAndWildcardIds][[timer]], state=TIMED_WAITING, group=TGRP-TransportGetPipelineActionTests]
        at java.base@17.0.2/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Native Method)
        at app//org.elasticsearch.threadpool.ThreadPool$CachedTimeThread.run(ThreadPool.java:671)

	at __randomizedtesting.SeedInfo.seed([DACFC603D5697F8A]:0)
```
It looks like there is a ThreadPool instance that hasn't been shut down at the end of the test? Though I'm not seeing one set up at all - perhaps its something downstream of some classes in the test?

Ah, found it - it's the NoOpClient - it creates a TestThreadPool instance which is leaving a timer thread laying about at the end of the test. Solution is simple - close the NoOpClient in a try-with-resources block

timeline.body: Looking good! Left a few comments

reply.body: Can you plz explain what is happening behind the scene?

The thread leak detection is taking a snapshot of all threads currently created before the test and when the test completes. If there are any threads that are left lying around, it throws an assertion error. Hence the failures. 

The `getMockClient()` method is returning a new instance of `NoOpClient`. Inside of its constructor, it is creating a new instance of `TestThreadPool` which is a subclass of `ThreadPool`. The `ThreadPool` instance creates a number of executors, schedulers, and threads (like the time caching thread). All of those threads need to be shutdown before the end of the test case. Putting client in the try-with-resources block will ensure that the client is closed after the block, which will close the thread pool underneath.
Removed this line while resolving conflicts with upstream.
